Seif 1, "all the needs of brit milah are performed on Shabbos," etc. Regarding whether only 2 mohalim or 3 should participate, Yeshuot Yaakov writes here that the common formulation is mistaken. I discussed the reason at length in a responsum to the community of Barzan, printed in my addenda to Niddah 19, page 113.

Regarding the dispute of Baal HaMaor and Ramban, cited by Ran in Perek R' Eliezer deMilah, where the hot water needed for the brit milah was spilled, the question is whether we judge the situation according to its present permitted state or according to the later consequence that will require desecration of Shabbos. I discussed this at length in my responsum to Lvov in the second addenda to Hilchot Shevuot, siman 239.

There is support from Niddah 38a concerning the early pious men, who would refrain from marital relations from Wednesday onward lest childbirth occur on Shabbos and lead to desecration of Shabbos. Why did they not say that the present act is entirely permitted and any later pikuach nefesh will itself override Shabbos? Evidently, where one knows that the present act will bring about later desecration, there can be a prohibition already at the outset. If they were stringent even where childbirth was only a possibility, this makes sense because certainty would have created an actual prohibition. But if certainty itself were completely permitted, there would be no reason for them to be stringent merely because of a doubt.

The proof of Baal HaMaor from slaughter on Yom Tov can be answered according to Ramban if Ramban holds that pikuach nefesh is hutrah rather than merely dechuyah. Covering blood after slaughter is permitted only because a positive commandment displaces a prohibition, which is merely a case of dechuyah; therefore before slaughter, when the need for that displacement can still be avoided, one must avoid creating it. Pikuach nefesh on Shabbos, however, would be completely permitted, and therefore the present act may be judged according to its current status. Baal HaMaor, who treats pikuach nefesh as dechuyah, can properly compare the cases.

Ran appears to rule that we consider the later consequence rather than only the present moment, except that he distinguishes brit milah, whose time is fixed on Shabbos, from Yom Tov slaughter. At first glance this conflicts with Ran's own words in Nedarim 16 concerning substitutes for prohibited benefit, where it appears that one may initially borrow even though the creditor will later collect from the prohibited property, because the present act contains no benefit and the later collection is treated as an after-the-fact situation. It seems necessary to distinguish Torah prohibitions from rabbinic prohibitions. The issue in Nedarim is only rabbinic, so there we judge according to the present moment. In the Shabbos and Yom Tov cases, where a Torah prohibition may later result, we consider the eventual consequence.

This distinction is a significant general principle in many areas. Taz in Yoreh De'ah, siman 117, concerning killing goats for commerce, also appears to follow the approach that we judge according to the present permitted state. His words can be upheld according to those who hold that the prohibition of commerce in neveilot is rabbinic.

Rambam writes in chapter 2 of Hilchot Shegagot, law 8: if a person had 2 infants, 1 whose brit milah was due on Shabbos and 1 whose brit milah was due on Friday or Sunday, and he forgot and performed both procedures on Shabbos, he is exempt from a sin-offering because he had permission to perform the procedure on 1 of them on Shabbos, Shabbos was displaced for him, and he performed a positive mitzvah, even though the 2 infants are separate bodies.

Rambam's wording, "Shabbos was displaced for him," requires explanation. Once he already stated that he had permission to perform 1 brit milah on Shabbos, why add that Shabbos was dechuyah for him, and why use the emphatic wording "for him"? It appears that Rambam intends to distinguish this from cases in which Shabbos is completely permitted.

Regarding communal impurity we rule that tumah is dechuyah rather than hutrah, and regarding a dangerously ill person Rambam likewise treats Shabbos as dechuyah. By contrast, the fixed Temple offerings of Shabbos are a case of hutrah. One must therefore determine the status of brit milah on Shabbos. Rambam's language indicates that brit milah too is a case of dechuyah, not hutrah.

This resolves the difficulty from the Gemara's comparison between brit milah and sacrificial limbs according to the opinions that treat tumah and Shabbos differently. The Gemara's challenge can be understood according to the view that tumah is hutrah for the public and that Shabbos in the Temple is likewise hutrah, or according to Abaye's principle that "since it became permitted, it remains permitted" is strong enough to support the comparison. We, however, rule that tumah is dechuyah for the public and that Shabbos is dechuyah for a dangerously ill person, and brit milah likewise is dechuyah. We also follow Rava's distinction that "since it was displaced, it remains displaced," but do not broadly apply "since it became permitted, it remains permitted."

Rambam is therefore exact. There are multiple grounds for exemption: the person had authority to perform a brit milah on Shabbos, Shabbos was in a state of dechuyah for him rather than complete prohibition, and he performed an actual positive mitzvah. This, in my view, is the proper understanding of Rambam at present.

(1) "On Shabbos." The verse states, "And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut," from which the Sages derive: on the eighth day, even when it is Shabbos. [Gemara]

(2) "And one performs metzitzah." Although metzitzah detaches blood from its place and would ordinarily constitute wounding, it is nevertheless performed because failure to draw out the blood poses danger to the infant. [Gemara]

(3) "Cumin." Their practice was to place a type of ground spice upon the site for healing. The same law applies to placing an isplenis, a medicinal dressing, upon the brit milah site. [Mishnah there] See below in seif 7 regarding a case where ground cumin had not been prepared before Shabbos.
